pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, with concrete numbers or mechanisms rather than slogans; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Why can a stateless service scale horizontally when a stateful one can't? Show me the line you deleted from `App` and tell me where that state went instead.
expected_points: any instance can serve any request, so the balancer can route freely and a dead instance loses only in-flight work
instance-local session map meant a token from instance 1 was invisible to instance 2
state moved to a shared store (Redis/database) or to a signed client-held token — it concentrates, it does not disappear
sticky sessions only paper over it: deploys log users out, instance death loses state, load can't be rebalanced, scale-in is destructive
same reasoning bans local disk and in-process counters that later requests depend on

questions.prompt: Explain your token bucket to me: what do `capacity` and `rate` each control, why is refill lazy, and what exactly does a rejected caller get back?
expected_points: rate is the sustained throughput promised; capacity is the burst tolerated (real clients are bursty)
lazy refill credits elapsed x rate on each call, capped at capacity — no background timer, O(1) state, testable with an injected clock
rejection is HTTP 429 (not 403 'never allowed', not 503 'server broken') with a Retry-After the client can trust
RetryAfter rounds up so waiting it guarantees success — a header that lies trains clients to ignore it
limits come from measured capacity and headroom, not invented numbers; observe in log-only mode before enforcing

questions.prompt: Your simulation ran 10 arrivals against 8 served per tick. Compare the bounded and unbounded backlogs at 100 and 1000 ticks, and tell me what those numbers mean for a user waiting on a response.
expected_points: bounded queue reaches a steady state — same backlog at 100 and 1000 ticks — and sheds the excess
unbounded backlog grows linearly with the length of the overload (10x the backlog at 10x the ticks)
Little's Law: wait = backlog / service rate, so a growing queue converts overload into unbounded latency and eventually OOM
an unbounded queue never rejects, so it never signals the problem; bounding turns a silent failure into a fast, visible one
on full: shed with 429/503 (cheapest work first, never health checks) or block the producer to push pressure upstream; bound in-flight concurrency too

questions.prompt: Walk me through how your ring assigns a key to a worker, why virtual nodes are there, and what happens the moment a worker dies.
expected_points: key and nodes hash onto a ring; the key belongs to the first node clockwise, found by binary search with a wrap to index 0
hash mod N reshuffles nearly every key when N changes; the ring moves only ~1/N and only onto the new node
virtual nodes (many positions per physical node) even out random arc sizes so each node's share converges on 1/N, and let you weight capacity
on death the dead node's arcs go to many different survivors instead of one neighbour, so the load spike is spread
the hash must be deterministic across processes and avalanche, or sequential keys clump
ownership is reassigned in milliseconds but is not durability — state that lived only in that worker needs replication

questions.prompt: You deploy that limiter to ten instances, each configured at 100 requests/second per tenant. What limit does a tenant actually get, and what are your options?
expected_points: 1000/s — per-instance limiters multiply by fleet size
shared counter (Redis): correct, but a network hop per request and its availability becomes yours
divide by instance count: no hop, wrong whenever the balancer is uneven or the fleet resizes
route a tenant's traffic to one instance by consistent hash so the local counter is the global one

questions.prompt: One tenant is 30% of your traffic and every request for them hits the same key. Does adding virtual nodes help? What does?
expected_points: no — the ring balances keys, and the key is the indivisible unit; a hot key lands on one node however fine the arcs are
split the key itself (user42#0..#9) or replicate/cache it on every node
related blast-radius idea: shuffle sharding gives each tenant a random small subset so no two tenants share their whole subset
recognises that scaling out also has limits from serial fractions (Amdahl) and coordination cost
